content: Chronic lung disease in individuals living with HIV can not only limit their full lung potential but also increase the risk of long-term respiratory complications in adulthood. A study conducted in South Africa observed a decline in lung function over two years among adolescents aged 9–16 years living with HIV, despite being on well-established antiretroviral therapy (ART). Diagnostic tools for chronic lung disease, such as spirometry and high-resolution computed tomography, are often unavailable in low-income settings. Consequently, chronic respiratory symptoms are frequently treated empirically with repeated courses of antibiotics and anti-tuberculosis therapy in regions with high HIV and TB prevalence. There are currently no specific guidelines for managing chronic lung disease associated with HIV. However, preventing lung infections through routine vaccinations (e.g., pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and annual influenza vaccine), early initiation of ART, continued co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, isoniazid preventive therapy, avoiding exposure to tobacco smoke and indoor air pollution, and optimizing nutrition can help reduce the burden of chronic lung disease and improve lung health in children living with HIV. Neurodevelopmental delays, neurocognitive disorders, and mental health issues are common among children living with HIV, particularly those who initiate ART after infancy. A prospective study of children aged 5–11 years from four sub-Saharan African countries revealed that children living with HIV performed worse across all cognitive domains compared to children who were either HIV-exposed but uninfected or HIV-unexposed. Despite more than 95% of these children achieving suppressed HIV viral loads and good immune status, only 1% had started ART within the first six months of life. The causes of neurocognitive impairment, even with effective ART, are likely multifactorial, including ongoing viral replication in the central nervous system (CNS), neuroinflammation, irreversible CNS injury prior to ART initiation, neurotoxic effects of ART, and compounding socioeconomic and psychosocial factors. Neurocognitive deficits in children may go unnoticed during routine testing, as they can appear asymptomatic. Context-specific and culturally validated screening tools and standardized definitions are scarce. A 2019 study in South Africa validated an international HIV dementia screening tool for young people. Mental health disorders, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), are highly prevalent among children and adolescents living with HIV, with higher rates observed in adolescents compared to younger children. These disorders often co-occur and are associated with poorer functional competence, self-concept, motivation, and higher levels of depression, disruptive behavior, and clinically significant anger compared to HIV-negative peers. Recurrent psychosocial stressors, such as stigma, discrimination, parental illness or death, and unstable guardianship, further exacerbate mental health vulnerabilities in children living with HIV. Mental health disorders can impair ART adherence and quality of life but often receive less attention than physical health concerns. Since up to half of adult mental health problems begin during childhood or adolescence, it is critical to implement mental health screening during adolescence. Promoting mental health and preventing mental health disorders are increasingly emphasized, with opportunities to integrate psychosocial support and mental health care at key points, such as during HIV status disclosure. Children living with HIV who experience advanced immunosuppression before initiating ART or who start ART at an older age are at an increased risk of developing cancer compared to those with milder immunosuppression or those who began ART in infancy. Data from five ART programs and four pediatric oncology units in South Africa reported an overall cancer incidence of 82 per 100,000 person-years, with Kaposi’s sarcoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma being the most common types. Although the incidence of AIDS-defining cancers has declined in the ART era, the risk of non-AIDS-defining cancers remains unchanged, highlighting the need for continued monitoring of children growing up with HIV. Multimorbidity is increasingly observed among young adults living with HIV on ART, particularly in younger age groups (18–35 and 36–45 years) compared to older adults (46–55 years). Adolescents with perinatally acquired HIV may face an elevated risk of multimorbidity as they age, especially in resource-limited settings where primary prevention of noncommunicable diseases and management of inflammatory coinfections are often inadequate. Service delivery platforms for children and adolescents living with HIV can be leveraged to screen for and manage noncommunicable diseases. For children under five years, early childhood development programs, under-five clinics, and HIV services can be utilized. For children aged 5–9 years, integrated school and HIV services are effective, while adolescent-friendly services are suitable for those aged 10–19 years. Despite challenges in implementing screening and prevention of noncommunicable diseases, opportunities exist to integrate these efforts into existing adolescent health activities. Some clinics have established adolescent groups to address various health issues, leveraging the regular interaction of adolescents living with HIV with the healthcare system to adopt a more comprehensive approach to health. Comprehensive HIV care for children and adolescents includes early ART initiation to prevent complications, monitoring growth and neurocognitive development, screening for organ-specific diseases, assessing psychosocial and mental health status, managing common mental health disorders, optimizing nutrition, ensuring vaccinations (e.g., pneumococcal, influenza, and HPV), cervical cancer screening after sexual debut, and referring to clinical specialties when necessary. Additionally, linking to community-based psychosocial support services and leveraging early childhood development platforms can support children living with HIV. Research priorities include understanding the epidemiology and pathogenesis of noncommunicable diseases in children and adolescents living with HIV, developing population-specific definitions of comorbidities, and identifying optimal screening and management strategies. Validated, age-appropriate, and culturally relevant screening tools for mental health and neurocognitive disorders are needed. Further research on prevention and treatment interventions, including antibiotics, antivirals, anti-inflammatory drugs, and vitamin D, as well as educational and mental health interventions, is essential. The interactions of antiretroviral drugs in children also require further study.
